options.text: the quantity of charge stored in a cell
the rate of flow of electric charge
the work done per unit charge
the opposition to the flow of charge

questions.explanation: Current is charge per unit time: $I = Q/t$. Its SI unit, the ampere, is one coulomb per second. Work done per unit charge is potential difference, and opposition to the flow of charge is resistance.

distractorRationale.a: Charge stored is Q, measured in coulombs, not current
distractorRationale.c: Work per unit charge is the definition of potential difference (the volt)
distractorRationale.d: Opposition to charge flow is resistance, measured in ohms

questions.stem: Ohm's law states that the current through a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it provided that

options.text: the length of the conductor is constant
the temperature of the conductor is constant
the cross-sectional area is constant
the conductor is in the shape of a wire

questions.explanation: Ohm's law is $V \propto I$ (or $V = IR$ with R constant) only at constant temperature. If the conductor heats up, as a lamp filament does, R itself changes and the I–V graph is no longer a straight line through the origin.

distractorRationale.a: Length affects the value of R but is not the condition that must be held constant for Ohm's law to apply as a statement of proportionality
distractorRationale.c: Area likewise affects R, but Ohm's law can be tested on a conductor of any fixed area
distractorRationale.d: The law applies to metallic conductors generally, not only to wires

questions.stem: A current of 2.5 A flows through a wire for 4.0 minutes. Calculate the quantity of charge that passes a point in the wire. Give your answer in coulombs.
questions.explanation: First convert the time: $4.0\ \text{min} = 4.0 \times 60 = 240\ \text{s}$. Then $Q = It = 2.5 \times 240 = 600\ \text{C}$. Leaving the time in minutes would give 10 C, which is far too small for a current of a few amperes lasting several minutes.

questions.stem: A 12 Ω resistor carries a current of 0.50 A. The potential difference across it is
questions.explanation: Ohm's law gives $V = IR = 0.50 \times 12 = 6.0\ \text{V}$. The potential difference is the product of current and resistance, not their quotient or their sum.

distractorRationale.b: This is R/I = 12/0.50, inverting Ohm's law
distractorRationale.c: This is I/R = 0.50/12, again inverting the formula
distractorRationale.d: This is I + R, adding quantities that do not share a unit

questions.stem: Which of the following devices has an I–V characteristic that is a straight line through the origin?

options.text: A filament lamp
A semiconductor diode
A metal wire kept at constant temperature
A thermistor as it warms up

questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin means I is proportional to V, so R = V/I is constant — the definition of an ohmic conductor. A metal wire at constant temperature is the standard ohmic example. A lamp filament, a diode and a warming thermistor all have resistance that changes with current or temperature, so their graphs are curved.

distractorRationale.a: A filament heats as the current rises, so R increases and the graph curves towards the V-axis
distractorRationale.b: A diode conducts freely in one direction and almost not at all in the other, so its graph is highly non-linear
distractorRationale.d: A thermistor's resistance falls as it warms, so the graph is not a straight line through the origin

questions.stem: A uniform wire is 2.0 m long and has a cross-sectional area of $0.50\ \text{mm}^2$. If the resistivity of the material is $1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\,\text{m}$, calculate the resistance of the wire. Give your answer in ohms.
questions.explanation: Convert the area: $0.50\ \text{mm}^2 = 0.50 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$. Then $R = \frac{\rho l}{A} = \frac{(1.0 \times 10^{-6})(2.0)}{5.0 \times 10^{-7}} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{5.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.0\ \Omega$. Leaving the area in mm² would make R a million times too small.

questions.stem: A wire has resistance 8.0 Ω. If its length is doubled and its cross-sectional area is halved, the new resistance is
questions.explanation: Since $R = \rho l / A$, doubling $l$ multiplies R by 2 and halving $A$ multiplies R by another 2, so the new resistance is $2 \times 2 = 4$ times the old one: $4 \times 8.0 = 32\ \Omega$. Resistivity is a property of the material and is unchanged.

distractorRationale.a: This halves the resistance, as if length were halved and area doubled — the inverse of the changes given
distractorRationale.b: This assumes the two changes cancel, which they would only if both were scaled by the same factor in ways that keep l/A constant
distractorRationale.c: This accounts for only one of the two changes (either doubling l or halving A, but not both)

questions.stem: The I–V graph of a filament lamp is a curve that becomes less steep as the potential difference increases. This is because

options.text: the current is inversely proportional to the potential difference
the resistance of the filament increases as its temperature rises
the filament obeys Ohm's law more closely at higher voltages
charge carriers are used up as the current grows

questions.explanation: On a graph of I against V the gradient is 1/R. A falling gradient therefore means R is rising. The lamp filament is a metal; metals increase in resistance as they get hotter, and a larger current dissipates more power ($I^2 R$) as heat. That is why a filament is a standard non-ohmic device.

distractorRationale.a: Current still increases with V; it just increases more slowly. Inverse proportion would make I fall as V rose
distractorRationale.c: The opposite is true: the graph is closest to a straight line at low V, before the filament has heated
distractorRationale.d: Charge is conserved and is not used up; the same electrons keep drifting around the circuit
